Labeling and Administration: Identifiers, Placement, and Records

Unit 1: Field Planning. Lesson 7 of 52 in INST1 Academy.

Eight months after you leave, a tech stands in the TR with a dead data port and 400 cables that look alike. The label is the only thing standing between that tech and an all-day trace. You are labeling for a stranger.

Why administration matters

Administration is the system of identifiers, labels, drawings, and records that makes a cabling system manageable. It follows one consistent scheme across the whole job, set by the specification or the designer, and you follow it exactly.

What gets an identifier

Every space, panel, port, cable, pathway, and bonding conductor gets a unique identifier.

Item           Example pattern                    Meaning
Space          3A                                 floor 3, telecom room A
Panel + port   3A-PP2-14                          room 3A, patch panel 2, port 14
Cable          3A-PP2-14 / 3-306-B                names both ends: panel and outlet
Outlet         3-306-B                            floor 3, room 306, port B
Bonding        3A-SBB1                            conductor to secondary busbar

A cable identifier names both ends, so the tech holding either end knows the other.

The rules

  • Label both ends of every cable with the same identifier.
  • Place the label within sight of the end, where it can be read without moving the cable.
  • Use machine-printed, durable labels. Handwriting smudges, and tape flags fall off.
  • Label bonding conductors at both ends too.

Records

The four administration classes, at recognition level, grow with the system: one telecom room, one building, a campus, and several campuses. The larger the system, the more records it needs. At closeout hand over the as-built drawings, the panel and cable records, and the test results, all agreeing with the labels.

Tip: print labels in the order you will pull, then check the first and last against the drawing before applying any.
Exam tip: a label that disagrees with the drawing or the panel record is a defect; the FIRST step is to confirm which one is right, then correct the rest.
Remember
One scheme, a unique identifier for everything, both ends labeled, machine printed, and records that agree with the labels.

This lesson includes an interactive lab in the course.

Deeper explanation

Labeling and Administration: Identifiers, Placement, and Records, explained slowly

One cable, labeled end to end

The best way to learn a labeling scheme is to label one cable from the TR to the outlet. Take a Category 6A cable to outlet B in room 306 on the third floor, landing on port 14 of the second patch panel in TR 3A. Here is the scheme this job uses, from the specification.

Item              Pattern                Example
Space             floor + letter         3A
Panel             room - panel           3A-PP2
Panel port        panel - port           3A-PP2-14
Outlet            floor - room - port    3-306-B
Cable             panel port / outlet    3A-PP2-14 / 3-306-B

The full label set

Where the label goes               Text on it
Cable at the TR end, near the panel 3A-PP2-14 / 3-306-B
Patch panel port 14                3A-PP2-14
Cable at the outlet end            3A-PP2-14 / 3-306-B
Faceplate, port B                  3-306-B
Pathway where cable enters         3A-C1 (conduit 1)
Bonding conductor to the SBB       3A-SBB1 at both ends

Both ends carry the same cable identifier, which names both ends. A tech who finds only the TR end knows the outlet, and a tech who finds only the outlet knows the panel and port.

Placing the label

Put it within sight of the end, where it reads without moving the cable. Wrap it around the jacket so it faces out, not under a bundle. Use a machine-printed, durable label. A handwritten label smudges and a flag label falls off.

Worked example

You test the cable and save the result using the identifier 3A-PP2-14 / 3-306-B. The tester file, the panel record, the drawing, and the label now all say the same thing. If any one disagrees, the record is wrong and an inspector or a tech will find it.

The four classes and closeout

Administration scales from one telecom room to several campuses. At closeout hand over the labeled records, the as-built drawings, and the test results.

Remember: one scheme, both ends, machine printed, and all four records agree.
